It takes a couple of days for a crematorium to reduce somebody to ashes.

I worked as a cremationist and it doesn't take days to reduce someone to ash. The average person up to 300lbs takes around 3.5 hours of burn time and another 2-3 hours to allow the retort to cool to a safe handling temperature.

A larger body or "wicker" takes around 1 hour and then then flame is turned off and the body is allowed to burn for roughly 3 hours on its own fats. Then the flame is turned back on and usually they are burned for 2-3 additional hours. Once the burn and cooling phase is completed, the remains are pushed out through a small door in the back. (modern retorts even have drop trays making it easier to remove).

The remains are then mostly ash and bone fragments, small parts of femurs, some rib fragments etc... They are taken and placed on a cooling table and allowed to fully cool down for around 2hrs. The remains are sifted through to ensure all foreign objects are removed (pieces of slag, medical implants, metal buttons from pants or shirts, etc...)

Then the remains are placed in a big pot looking blender with a titanium blade in it. They are processed further into a finer powder for roughly 3-5min. The remains are then bagged and tagged and presented to the funeral homes that dropped them off in a plastic urn. The funeral homes will either transfer the remains into their own urns or do what they do with them from that point on.

If you burned a body in a modern retort for more than 6hrs there would be no bone fragments to process depending on bone density. I've burned 400lb guys that filled up the same amount of the urn as a 90lb lady oddly enough...

Usually what we do when firing up a retort with a body inside is we ensure there are no errors displayed on the panel and then we gtfo out of there for a while. In my case, I would load an individual into the retort and ensure that the unit got to 365° without any warnings or issues. From that point on our unit would go beast mode and temp climbs very fast.

The reason for leaving right away is that not all bodies come in at the same stage and some are filled with gases etc... When they heat up rapidly they can pop, hiss, outright explode basically. You don't want to be around to hear high pitched screaming type sounds or what it sounds like when a body pops.

Once the burners kicked on full steam I would leave. The unit will climb to 1700°f pretty quickly from the lower temp while it's still ok to be around. Typically, it's required that the retort is checked every hour or at a minimum half way through the process to ensure it's safe and there hasn't been any faults.

If the panel trips or the blower goes out or there is a ignitor or gas issue it can be a bad time. You have to open the unit and inspect where in the process they left off and get the unit back up and finish processing the remains. There is a peep hole on the unit like on a front door of a house that allows the operator to inspect for flame but you cannot inspect the body or see it through the peep sight.

There is also the real danger of fire if the body isn't positioned correctly or if the fats escape the retort as a result of poor placement. "Wickers" or larger individuals are placed in head first to prevent their fats from draining out and igniting.

The unit itself is normally housed in an area that prevents a fire from spreading but the entire unit could be destroyed if someone fucks up. Also, there are weight limits for retorts and special retorts for people over 600 lbs. No one wants to spend time scrubbing people grease off a unit with 409 kitchen cleaner.

There are laws on things like not being able to process animal remains in the same unit as humans etc...

As for your original question about the smells. There are a lot of circumstances that vary and the smells too. Bodies depending on how they are received vary on smell. Someone who just died at the old age home and is brought over ready to go typically don't have much smell at all.

Most times a body is in a body bag and are processed as such. There are basically large cardboard boxes with no lid that are assembled and the covered body or body bag is placed in that for processing. On rare occasions they might arrive covered in linens, clothing or in a burnable casket.

All bodies are treated with the utmost of respect and always have to be covered no matter what. You don't burn naked bodies etc...

Some people come from the coroner's office and might not have been found for some time. Those are pretty bad smelling even bagged, they que first.

Some types of diseases or cancers really take a toll on a body. Some people are already beginning to break down before they even die just because the cancer eats them up etc... Those people also typically have a short que and smell even through the bag.

Some people come from the funeral home and might have been embalmed to some degree or kept in the cooler and they smell almost like a pine, mint type scent but not good. They que first come first serve usually unless someone else is worse off. They can keep in the body cooler for a day or two and wait their turns.

Some religious preferences can be difficult and can be really hard to deal with without getting ill. For instance, some Native American tribe might request that a body be left undisturbed for several days prior to processing. A funeral home may leave them out as per requested and then bring the body up to 4 days or so later to be processed. It's impossible to be around but not too many of those requests come often and they will make anyone want to stop doing the job. The only thing worse than processing those bodies is the poor guy driving them to you in a minivan.

Once the cremation starts it's not too bad. I worked at a cemetery/crematorium. We did grounds work between stages etc... When the box/clothing etc...begins to burn there will be a heavy smoke that comes out of the stack or flue.

We didn't process bodies on days there were funerals etc...so no one got hit by a cloud caught in the breeze. The smoke lasts for less than an hour normally the heaviest part is over within 15 minutes or so. If you work in that area and the smoke happens to hit you or you catch a whiff of it as it goes by it has its own distinct smell. It's like gunpowder and faintly like burnt hair.

Nothing really survives the process and any remains that go to the cooling table are brittle enough to break apart with two fingers. There isn't really any smell of anything once the remains are moved out. However, when the remains are in the blender they create some dust in the air. The unit has a filter and fan to suck most of the dust up but it can still be pretty palatable and dense.

Normally, I would begin that process, leave for a few minutes while it did it's thing and returned to inspect and finish processing them. No one wants to breath or be covered in people flour.

Hope that answers your questions.
